item.title: Why Video Compresses 100×: Redundancy, YUV, I/P/B Frames and GOP
item.description:
The later posts on browser codec selection and the streaming protocol panorama keep leaning on H.264, I-frames and GOP — this post fills in the foundation first: what actually happens when a stream of pixels turns into a few Mbps. No math derivations — mechanisms, each tied to its engineering consequence (latency, seeking, corruption, storage).

Start with some arithmetic.

How big is uncompressed video

One 1080p (1920×1080), 30fps, 8bit RGB stream:

text
1
2

pixels per frame = 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600
bytes per frame = 2,073,600 × 3 (RGB) ≈ 5.93 MB
per second = 5.93 MB × 30 ≈ 178 MB/s
bitrate ≈ 1.49 Gbps

That is 10.7 GB per minute. 4K (3840×2160) multiplies by another 4: ~42.7 GB/min. Sixteen surveillance cameras recording for a month at these rates is beyond any storage system. In practice 1080p surveillance streams run 2–8 Mbps — a compression ratio on the order of several hundred to one. Compression is not an optimization; it is the precondition for video existing at all.

item.title: Rescuing Picture Quality on a Weak Network: What Receiver-Side "Low-Res to HD" Can Actually Do
item.description:
A chain store’s cameras report over 4G; during the evening rush the picture smears into mush. A construction-site camera doesn’t have the uplink; the license plate in the recording is never legible. After reading a product brochure, the owner asks a natural question: AI can sharpen old photos now — can it sharpen my footage too?

The question deserves a real answer, because it isn’t a yes or a no. In October 2026 I traced this line from papers and open-source projects through commercial products to court rulings. The conclusion up front: receiver-side super-resolution helps with exactly one specific damage class; it cannot fix corruption or stutter; and in surveillance/forensics contexts it carries a legal red line. This post explains why, written for readers with no video-coding background — every term is explained where it first appears.
